title: Axiom
summary: Axiom is a long-running espionage cluster that public reporting has tracked since at least 2008, with most victim organisations in government, telecommunications, aerospace, defence and media. The group is known for combining website compromise with targeted intrusion: operators inject code into sites their targets are expected to visit, use that position to profile visitors, and only then decide who receives a payload. Persistence is usually established with custom back doors rather than commodity remote access tools, and command and control rides over ordinary web traffic so it blends with normal browsing. Evidence of Axiom activity typically appears as outbound requests from a workstation to a low-reputation site, unexplained processes with a stable beacon interval, and web server logs showing injected script on a site the organisation does not own. A common misunderstanding is that a watering hole attack requires the victim to download something obvious; in practice the first stage is silent profiling, and only carefully selected visitors ever receive the second stage. Attribution to a specific state sponsor rests on vendor reporting and is held with varying confidence.

beginner.definition: Axiom is the name security researchers use for a group of attackers who spy on governments and large companies. They have been active since around 2008. Researchers believe the group works for a national government, but this is an assessment rather than a proven fact.
beginner.whyItMatters: Groups like Axiom do not steal money from bank accounts. They quietly copy documents, email and plans over months or years. If you ignore this kind of activity, one small mistake on one laptop can lead to years of lost secrets. Knowing how these groups work helps you spot strange network traffic early.
howItWorks: The attackers pick websites that people in the target company often read, such as news pages or industry forums.
They break into that website and add hidden code, so the site still looks normal to everyone who visits it.
The hidden code checks each visitor and reports basic details back, such as the browser and the internet address.
Only visitors who match the target list receive the next step, which may be a fake update or a small program.
That program installs a quiet back door, which is a hidden way in, and it calls home on a schedule.
The operators then read files, collect email and move slowly, so the activity looks like normal business traffic.
beginner.example: Think of a busy coffee shop that a company's staff visit every morning. Someone quietly replaces the sugar packets with tiny tracking tags, but only for the people on a list. Everyone else drinks their coffee as usual and notices nothing at all. The staff who matter carry a tag home without realising it, and from then on a stranger knows exactly when they are at their desk. The shop never looks damaged, so the owner has no reason to inspect the sugar bowl.
takeaways: Spying groups often wait and collect quietly instead of causing damage you can see.
A website you trust can be changed so that it attacks only a few visitors.
Unusual traffic from your computer to a strange website is worth reporting.

objectives: Describe what an espionage intrusion group is and how it differs from a criminal group.
Explain how a watering hole attack profiles visitors before delivering a payload.
Identify the log and network evidence that a long-term back door leaves behind.
Explain why attribution to a national government is reported with limited confidence.
List practical defensive controls that reduce the value of a compromised website.
